papers.title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks
papers.authors: Alexandra Souly, Qingyuan Lu, Dillon Bowen, Tu Trinh et al.
papers.what: [Conference] Most jailbreak papers claim the jailbreaks they propose are highly effective, often boasting near-100% attack success rates. However, it is perhaps more common than not for jailbreak developers to substantially exaggerate the effectiveness of their jailbreaks. We suggest this pro
papers.summary: Most jailbreak papers claim the jailbreaks they propose are highly effective, often boasting near-100% attack success rates. However, it is perhaps more common than not for jailbreak developers to substantially exaggerate the effectiveness of their jailbreaks. We suggest this problem arises because jailbreak researchers lack a standard, high-quality benchmark for evaluating jailbreak performance, leaving researchers to create their own. To create a benchmark, researchers must choose a dataset of forbidden prompts to which a victim model will respond, along with an evaluation method that scores the harmfulness of the victim model's responses. We show that existing benchmarks suffer from significant shortcomings and introduce the StrongREJECT benchmark to address these issues. StrongREJECT's dataset contains prompts that victim models must answer with specific, harmful information, while its automated evaluator measures the extent to which a response gives useful information to forbidden prompts. In doing so, the StrongREJECT evaluator achieves state-of-the-art agreement with human judgments of jailbreak effectiveness. Notably, we find that existing evaluation methods significantly overstate jailbreak effectiveness compared to human judgments and the StrongREJECT evaluator. We describe a surprising and novel phenomenon that explains this discrepancy: jailbreaks bypassing a victim model's safety fine-tuning tend to reduce its capabilities. Together, our findings underscore the need for researchers to use a high-quality benchmark, such as StrongREJECT, when developing new jailbreak attacks. We release the StrongREJECT code and data at https://strong-reject.readthedocs.io/en/latest/.

papers.title: Gaussian Splatting SLAM
papers.authors: Hidenobu Matsuki, Riku Murai, Paul H. J. Kelly, Andrew J. Davison
papers.what: [Conference] We present the first application of 3D Gaussian Splatting in monocular SLAM, the most fundamental but the hardest setup for Visual SLAM. Our method, which runs live at 3fps, utilises Gaussians as the only 3D representation, unifying the required representation for accurate, effic
papers.summary: We present the first application of 3D Gaussian Splatting in monocular SLAM, the most fundamental but the hardest setup for Visual SLAM. Our method, which runs live at 3fps, utilises Gaussians as the only 3D representation, unifying the required representation for accurate, efficient tracking, mapping, and high-quality rendering. Designed for challenging monocular settings, our approach is seamlessly extendable to RGB-D SLAM when an external depth sensor is available. Several innovations are required to continuously reconstruct 3D scenes with high fidelity from a live camera. First, to move beyond the original 3DGS algorithm, which requires accurate poses from an offline Structure from Motion (SfM) system, we formulate camera tracking for 3DGS using direct optimisation against the 3D Gaussians, and show that this enables fast and robust tracking with a wide basin of convergence. Second, by utilising the explicit nature of the Gaussians, we introduce geometric verification and regularisation to handle the ambiguities occurring in incremental 3D dense reconstruction. Finally, we introduce afull SLAM system which not only achieves state-of-the-art results in novel view synthesis and trajectory estimation but also reconstruction of tiny and even transparent objects.

papers.title: TUTTI: Parallel CKKS Bootstrapping in under 3 ms on CPU
papers.authors: Robin Köstler, Antonio Guimarães
papers.what: [Explore] This paper introduces TUTTI, a new CKKS bootstrapping procedure that outperforms previous low-latency solutions in multi-threaded latency for any number of messages and, most notably, has a lower latency than TFHE when bootstrapping a single one. Our bootstrapping builds upon SPR
papers.summary: This paper introduces TUTTI, a new CKKS bootstrapping procedure that outperforms previous low-latency solutions in multi-threaded latency for any number of messages and, most notably, has a lower latency than TFHE when bootstrapping a single one. Our bootstrapping builds upon SPRU (CK, TCHES 2027), improving it with new methods for exploiting parallelism and increasing the number of messages, as well as with a refined security analysis, of independent interest, of the block-binary secret keys of LMSS (AsiaCCS 2023). TUTTI bootstraps 4096 real-number messages in 46 to 83.4 ms on 192 threads to restore 1 to 9 multiplicative levels, outperforming SHIP (CHKS, Eurocrypt 2025) by a factor of up to 3 on the same machine. Unlike SHIP, TUTTI gains immediately from bootstrapping fewer messages, with a 256-message bootstrapping taking just 15 to 34 ms on 32 threads. For a single message, TUTTI takes 4.6 ms on 32 threads, whereas TFHE-rs needs 7.3 ms for a 4-bit bootstrapping on the same machine and thread count. We show that this advantage persists across different architectures: on an Apple M5 Pro laptop (ARM), TUTTI takes 2.4 ms on 14 threads, against 4.5 ms for TFHE-rs. Differences between CKKS and lightweight schemes such as TFHE remain on several fronts, from functionality to key sizes and security assumptions, but our work shows that multi-threaded latency is no longer one of them, closing a long-standing gap in the practical FHE literature.

papers.title: Hidden Distances: How Likert-Scale Spacing Shapes Algorithmic Voting Advice
papers.authors: Thomas Broholt Knudsen, Christian Høst-Madsen, Vedran Sekara, Jonas L. Juul
papers.what: [Explore] Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) are algorithmic recommenders that match voters with political candidates on policy preferences. They are widely adopted across many multi-party democracies; in Denmark, 62\% of eligible voters used a VAA ahead of the 2022 general election, and 45
papers.summary: Voting Advice Applications (VAAs) are algorithmic recommenders that match voters with political candidates on policy preferences. They are widely adopted across many multi-party democracies; in Denmark, 62\% of eligible voters used a VAA ahead of the 2022 general election, and 45\% of VAA users reported following its advice. VAAs typically ask voters and candidates to respond to policy statements on a Likert scale, from ``strongly disagree'' to ``strongly agree'', and recommend candidates whose responses are closest to the voter's. Computing these distances requires assigning numbers to response options, a design choice without an empirical basis, since it is unknown how people perceive the distances between options. Here we show that this seemingly technical choice substantially changes whom voters are matched with. We parameterize the distance between ``(dis)agree'' and ``strongly (dis)agree'' relative to the distance between ``neutral'' and ``(dis)agree'' as $α$, and quantify how it changes recommendations for a popular Danish VAA. We find that moving from equidistant options to doubling this distance can change $37.7\%$ of top candidate matches and $21.9\%$ of top party matches, although no answers change. Low $α$-values favor candidates with strong positions, with some parties receiving up to $ 19.6\%$ more recommendations, while high $α$-values favor moderates. Similarly, female candidates receive fewer recommendations at low $α$ and more at high $α$-values. Our findings demonstrate that undisclosed quantification choices in algorithmic recommenders can carry considerable electoral consequences, and they call for transparency and sensitivity analysis in VAA design. As Likert-based matching also underpins dating platforms and roommate allocation systems, these implications extend well beyond elections.

papers.title: Creative Intent as an Evolving Shared State: Supporting Cross-Stage Human-AI Video Co-Creation
papers.authors: Yuhang Jin, Mengfei Chen, Hanwei Zheng, Songruoyao Wu et al.
papers.what: [Explore] As generative AI becomes increasingly involved in video creation, creators face challenges in expanding, translating, and negotiating creative intent across stages. We therefore view creative intent as an evolving shared state throughout human-AI co-creation. A multi-stage design
papers.summary: As generative AI becomes increasingly involved in video creation, creators face challenges in expanding, translating, and negotiating creative intent across stages. We therefore view creative intent as an evolving shared state throughout human-AI co-creation. A multi-stage design was employed: semi-structured interviews with 12 creators informed 3 design goals, followed by expert co-design and the development of VideoMaker. VideoMaker organizes creation into a six-stage workflow that progressively translates creative intent. At key stages, creators negotiate with AI through the Seed Panel, explicitly confirming, revising, and updating intent. A shared AI Agent, supported by the Multi-style Script Library and Cinematic Language Knowledge Base, enables differentiated expansion of initial intent and faithful translation. A within-subjects study with 30 participants showed that VideoMaker effectively supported the expansion and cross-stage translation of creative intent, with stronger intent preservation, while negotiated boundaries between creator-confirmed intent and AI initiative remained difficult to sustain.

papers.title: Maurer-Inspired Two-Way Physical-Layer Authentication Against Multi-Antenna Impersonation Attacks
papers.authors: Pin-Hsun Lin, Linda Senigagliesi, Eduard A. Jorswieck
papers.what: [Explore] In this work, we investigate Maurer-inspired two-way physical-layer authentication. Alice seeks authentication by Bob in the presence of a multi-antenna impersonator, Trudy. Trudy may replace the challenge to Alice, the response to Bob, or both. To create an information advantage
papers.summary: In this work, we investigate Maurer-inspired two-way physical-layer authentication. Alice seeks authentication by Bob in the presence of a multi-antenna impersonator, Trudy. Trudy may replace the challenge to Alice, the response to Bob, or both. To create an information advantage, Bob adds artificial noise (AN) to his challenge, and Alice adds spatial AN while forwarding the received mixture. Bob predicts the response from trusted preparation, whereas Trudy observes only a noisy version of the challenge, and Alice's AN interferes with Trudy's preparation reception. Impersonation thus requires matching Bob's fresh randomness beyond the channel consistency checked by public-pilot one-way authentication. For quasi-static Gaussian multiple-input multiple-output channels with time-division duplex (TDD) reciprocity, we derive missed-detection bounds for attacks that replace the authentication challenge, the response, or both. These bounds assume attack-free initial training and preparation and account for estimation error and AN leakage. With equal antenna numbers at all nodes, we show scenarios where the proposed scheme has lower worst-case missed detection than specified one-way tests with/without AN.

papers.title: Certifying the Error-Detection Value of Functional Dependencies without Ground Truth
papers.authors: Xiaolong Wan, Xixian Han
papers.what: [Explore] Functional dependencies are used to flag erroneous cells, but without error labels the value of these flags is unknown. Dependency strength cannot settle it, because identical data and flags can have positive value in one clean state and negative value in another. We treat this v
papers.summary: Functional dependencies are used to flag erroneous cells, but without error labels the value of these flags is unknown. Dependency strength cannot settle it, because identical data and flags can have positive value in one clean state and negative value in another. We treat this value as partially identified and certify a fixed detector when its value is positive in every clean state compatible with the observation under an error model and budget. The largest such budget is the certification radius. For a detector that flags departures from the unique mode of each class, the worst case reduces to a 0/1 knapsack over class flips, yielding sharp bounds on true positives and the exact radius in polynomial time. Allowing bounded legitimate exceptions in the clean data, we derive an exact threshold for the existence of a positive certificate and compute the radius with the same knapsack. Across five relations and 21,981 candidate dependencies, rules with nearly equal $g_3$ and flag rate can have certification margins differing tenfold. Error injection confirms sound certification and shows that, at equal error counts, changing the organization of errors reverses certification outcomes for every tested rule.

papers.title: When the Norm is Wrong: Social Norm Misspecification and Targeting with an Application to Microfinance Adoption
papers.authors: Shantanu Chadha
papers.what: [Explore] Structural models of peer effects typically capture peer influence through the average, aggregate, or in some cases through extreme peer actions. Such specifications, however, are imposed ex ante and are typically ad hoc. We study the consequences of social norm misspecification
papers.summary: Structural models of peer effects typically capture peer influence through the average, aggregate, or in some cases through extreme peer actions. Such specifications, however, are imposed ex ante and are typically ad hoc. We study the consequences of social norm misspecification by extending the constant elasticity of substitution (CES) norm from continuous to discrete choices. Considering a binary-choice game with incomplete information, we derive results on existence and uniqueness of a rational expectations equilibrium and establish conditions for identification of the structural parameters. We estimate the model by the Nested Pseudo-Likelihood estimator, implemented using the spectral algorithm. Monte Carlo simulations show that the CES estimates of the peer effects approach their true values as the sample grows, whereas imposing a linear norm biases them even in large samples. We apply the framework to microfinance adoption in India and find a strongly max-leaning norm, with significant heterogeneity in curvature and peer effects across villages grouped by caste composition and wealth. In a counterfactual exercise that allocates a fixed subsidy budget to maximise adoption, the estimated and linear norms target very different households, with the former favouring village "leaders", who are more likely to adopt and were the first to be informed about microfinance.

papers.title: The role of administrative costs in policies to improve cooperation
papers.authors: Giacomo Vaccario, Luca Verginer, Frank Schweitzer
papers.what: [Explore] We use an agent-based model for studying policies of an abstract government to increase the level of cooperation. In situations where defection is the rational choice, agents receive a bonus if they choose to cooperate. The government taxes agents' payoffs from a repeated prisone
papers.summary: We use an agent-based model for studying policies of an abstract government to increase the level of cooperation. In situations where defection is the rational choice, agents receive a bonus if they choose to cooperate. The government taxes agents' payoffs from a repeated prisoner's dilemma game to establish a budget that covers the payment of bonuses, but also the administrative costs involved. We consider costs to identify cooperators, and costs to mitigate the consequences of defective behavior. Governmental interventions are fallible, i.e. cooperators and defectors are correctly identified only with a certain accuracy. Hence, the critical bonus needed to let agents cooperate depends on the accuracy, but also on the current level of cooperation. We analyze the cost constraints for the government to pay the critical bonus and different policies to adjust the accuracy dependent on the level of cooperation. We find that perfect cooperation becomes impossible. Instead, high levels of cooperation can be achieved with optimal adjustment policies.

papers.title: OCEAN: A Five-Phase Framework for Meaningful Change
papers.authors: A. Fronzetti Colladon
papers.what: [Explore] Managing meaningful change requires more than motivation, insight, or isolated techniques. This paper introduces OCEAN, a five-phase conceptual framework for structuring nonclinical developmental conversations and change-oriented work in coaching and in the practice of leaders an
papers.summary: Managing meaningful change requires more than motivation, insight, or isolated techniques. This paper introduces OCEAN, a five-phase conceptual framework for structuring nonclinical developmental conversations and change-oriented work in coaching and in the practice of leaders and HR professionals. The five phases are Observe, Create, Expose, Awaken, and Nurture. In Observe, individuals develop a systemic, present-oriented understanding of the situation. In Create, they turn that understanding into goals that are meaningful and actionable. In Expose, they identify the attempted solutions that maintain the difficulty they are meant to remove, along with the resistances, biases, and self-deceptions that keep them in place. In Awaken, they activate new behaviors through planning, reframing, paradoxical movement, and emotionally significant experiences. In Nurture, they consolidate progress through repetition, habits, connection, and sustainable contexts. OCEAN integrates insights from systemic and interactional thinking, goal construction, emotional awareness, and habit consolidation into a structured process.

papers.title: Certified Zonotopic Reachability Analysis for Trajectory Tracking on Lie Groups
papers.authors: Yanliang Huang, Peng Xie, Zhen Zhang, Zhuoqi Zeng et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Autonomous vehicles track planned trajectories close to obstacles. Unknown disturbances make them deviate from these trajectories. With a bound on the tracking error that disturbances can cause, a planned trajectory can be certified as safe before execution. Existing set-based me
papers.summary: Autonomous vehicles track planned trajectories close to obstacles. Unknown disturbances make them deviate from these trajectories. With a bound on the tracking error that disturbances can cause, a planned trajectory can be certified as safe before execution. Existing set-based methods bound the tracking error by one invariant ellipsoid for the whole trajectory or by intervals, which are both conservative. For aerial and space vehicles, the tracking error evolves on a matrix Lie group with nonlinear dynamics. However, for group-affine systems, the error dynamics are linear in Lie algebra coordinates when the vehicle receives the inputs of the reference. The control input and the disturbance enter through the inverse right Jacobian, a matrix that depends on the error. We propagate the linear part of the error dynamics with zonotopes and enclose the effect of the inverse right Jacobian on the disturbance in closed form. The resulting tubes are tight and provably contain all reachable tracking errors in continuous time. When some error components have no input, the inverse right Jacobian leaves unmatched nonlinear terms in the closed loop. None of the tested methods certifies such a closed loop. Hybrid coordinates make these terms matched, so that our controller cancels every nonlinear term that does not contain the disturbance. Our tubes give tighter bounds than the ellipsoid method in simulations of a planar aircraft and a fully actuated multirotor and in real flights of a quadrotor, where the tube contains every measured attitude error. Under larger disturbances and the same feedback gain, the ellipsoid method yields no valid ellipsoid, whereas our tubes remain valid.

papers.title: BioBind: Binding Biometric Deduplication to Zero-Knowledge Authentication
papers.authors: Taotao Wang, Xiaoxiao Wu, Shengli Zhang
papers.what: [Explore] Biometric identity systems for decentralized applications need credentials that resist repeated enrollment and support private, publicly verifiable authentication. Capture and large-scale private deduplication run off chain while smart contracts authorize issuance and use; these
papers.summary: Biometric identity systems for decentralized applications need credentials that resist repeated enrollment and support private, publicly verifiable authentication. Capture and large-scale private deduplication run off chain while smart contracts authorize issuance and use; these stages span distinct trust domains, and a correct verdict covers only the checked inputs and gallery snapshot. Without binding and state checks, concurrent enrollments can issue duplicate credentials from correct verdicts, while substituted inputs can authorize unrelated credentials. We present BioBind, a protocol whose four backend interface conditions bind the deduplication query, gallery insertion and issued commitment to one captured vector, authenticate gallery transitions, and require a sound uniqueness verdict valid at finalization. Its encrypted instance uses bound requests, stale-session rejection and committee-confirmed migration. Capture-bound zero-knowledge authentication links credential use to the enrolled template and a fresh device-originated probe bound to the challenge. We give a conditional multi-session composition argument under explicit capture, backend and cryptographic assumptions. A prototype using LFW face features rejects the tested composition attacks; its unlinkable authentication circuit uses 31,445 constraints and about 305,000 gas. An equal-public-field baseline quantifies the cost of verifiable matching: witness-plus-proving medians are 1.989 s versus 1.119 s with device-trusted matching. Separate tests of encrypted enrollment complete three histories of 16,384 registrations without decoding errors at the tested checkpoints. Biometric accuracy bounds person-level uniqueness: on the Bosphorus database, cooperative subjects who change appearance evade deduplication in 1.8% of re-enrollment attempts at the operating threshold. Full backend integration remains open.

papers.title: Causal Resolution of Undefined Answers in Datalog with Negation
papers.authors: Ratan Bahadur Thapa
papers.what: [Explore] Unstratified negation may leave the answer to a Boolean Datalog query undefined under the well-founded semantics. We study database causality in this setting by asking which fact insertions and deletions realize a prescribed transition and which other changes preserve the observe
papers.summary: Unstratified negation may leave the answer to a Boolean Datalog query undefined under the well-founded semantics. We study database causality in this setting by asking which fact insertions and deletions realize a prescribed transition and which other changes preserve the observed query answer while making a designated fact pivotal. Such a set of changes to other facts is a contingency for the designated fact and the prescribed transition. Our game representation assigns one shared move to each mutable fact and preserves query values and intervention distances. Pairing source and target certificates characterizes all minimum contingencies for the six transitions among true, false, and undefined. When inserting or deleting a move resolves a draw, a directed tree traces the newly winning and losing positions along alternating paths to the source of that move. For the fixed one-rule win--move program, deciding whether a contingency of size at most $k$ exists is $\mathrm{NP}$-complete for each transition, even on bounded-degree graphs. Computing the minimum size is $\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{NP}[\log]}$-complete, and counting minimum contingencies is $\#\mathrm{P}$-hard under polynomial-time Turing reductions. When only one of true and false is reachable, the prime implicants of undefinedness satisfied at the observation cover every undefined state, and their supports induce nonempty subtrees of a common tree, we compute a minimum resolving intervention in polynomial time from the game instance. From the explicit tree and these implicants, we construct an equally large family of disjoint supports, certifying optimality.

papers.title: Average versus expected causal effects under interference: Modeling assumptions and estimation bottlenecks
papers.authors: Vishesh Karwa, Edoardo M. Airoldi, Donald B. Rubin
papers.what: [Explore] Causal inference under treatment interference requires assumptions to reduce the exponentially large number of potential outcomes. We develop hierarchical finite-population models for potential outcomes by separating these assumptions into three layers: interference neighborhoods
papers.summary: Causal inference under treatment interference requires assumptions to reduce the exponentially large number of potential outcomes. We develop hierarchical finite-population models for potential outcomes by separating these assumptions into three layers: interference neighborhoods, exposure mappings, and outcome models. Given an interference neighborhood and exposure mapping, we show that potential outcomes admit a nonparametric decomposition into direct, spillover, and treatment--spillover interaction components. This decomposition provides a common coordinate system for nonparametric, semiparametric, and parametric models of finite-population potential outcomes. For a given potential-outcome model, we define two classes of estimands. Average causal effects (ACEs), such as direct and total treatment effects, contrast potential outcomes under fixed treatment--exposure conditions. Expected causal effects (ECEs), such as expected direct and indirect effects, contrast expectations of potential outcomes under a specified allocation policy. For both classes, we bound the variance of the canonical Horvitz--Thompson estimator by three terms: a diagonal weight term, a term from overlapping interference neighborhoods, and a residual design-dependence term. Our upper and lower bounds show that under graph-unaware designs, nonparametric design-unbiased estimation of ACEs can require sample sizes growing exponentially in the interference degree, whereas polynomial growth can suffice for design-aligned ECEs. Under neighborhood interference, we construct graph-aware independent-set designs with variance bounds polynomial in the maximum degree for direct and total treatment effects on every graph, whereas graph cluster randomization can incur worst-case variance exponential in the degree.

papers.title: Retweeting patterns reveal partisan asymmetries in information sharing and signal state-level electoral outcomes in the 2020 US presidential election
papers.authors: Dawei Li, Qinjun Wan, Xin Wang, Dahe Jiang et al.
papers.what: [Explore] As social media has become a primary source of political information, concerns are growing that online information consumption may intensify political polarization and reshape democratic processes. Yet how large-scale online information consumption organizes polarized political e
papers.summary: As social media has become a primary source of political information, concerns are growing that online information consumption may intensify political polarization and reshape democratic processes. Yet how large-scale online information consumption organizes polarized political ecosystems and relates to offline voting remains unclear. Here we reconstruct partisan information ecosystems from more than 500 million tweets generated during the 2020 US presidential election, integrating information diffusion across media outlets, influencers, and social peers. Contrary to the conventional expectation that broader information exposure promotes moderation, we find that retweeting a wider range of political information is associated with stronger political polarization. We further show systematic asymmetries in political information ecosystems: the Republican ecosystem is highly concentrated and ideologically biased, whereas the Democratic ecosystem is more dispersed and primarily organized around relatively moderate left-leaning sources. Finally, we demonstrate that several shared retweeting signatures robustly map onto state-level electoral outcomes despite cross-state heterogeneity. Our findings reveal asymmetric political information ecosystems as a key organizing principle of online political communication and identify collective retweeting patterns as a scalable signal of real-world voting behaviours.

papers.title: Modelling socio-economic effects of the pandemic in a metropolitan area
papers.authors: Jan E. Snellman, Rafael A. Barrio, Cecilia I. Ventura, Tzipe Govezensky et al.
papers.what: [Explore] One of the most notorious measures taken by authorities in every country trying to prevent the uncontrollable spread of the Covid 19 pandemic was to impose severe measures to diminish the mobility of people. In recent publications we proposed a mathematical model to address the c
papers.summary: One of the most notorious measures taken by authorities in every country trying to prevent the uncontrollable spread of the Covid 19 pandemic was to impose severe measures to diminish the mobility of people. In recent publications we proposed a mathematical model to address the consequences of these measures and to predict the infections under different scenarios, for various different countries. In this paper we extend the model, called the BTH--SEIRS-model, to deal with the reduction of mobility in an urban area. The chosen region was the densely-populated metropolitan area around Helsinki, the capital of Finland. This choice obeyed to the fact that there are precise data related to mobility from a mobile telephone company, and that this region was completely isolated from the rest of the country for a short period during the pandemic. We also used public transport data from railways and the accommodation occupation rates in the area of interest. We show that the BTH--SEIRS model is capable of simulating the real infection data as well as the mobility-related economic activity, exhibiting the main trends present in the three indicators used for comparison. Our calculations allow us to highlight the difference of the behaviour of the pandemic in a totally different spatial scale, and to discover the hidden factors that govern the behaviour of people who are forced to commute every day from home to work.

papers.title: Executable Human Study Programs with Silicon Participants
papers.authors: Xuan Liu, Haoyang Shang, Yuanjun Feng, Shao-Yu Chu et al.
papers.what: [Explore] We introduce HumanStudyProgram, a framework that represents a documented human study as an executable program with configurable LLM-based silicon participants. Its computational abstraction separates study logic from participant implementation through standardized APIs for presen
papers.summary: We introduce HumanStudyProgram, a framework that represents a documented human study as an executable program with configurable LLM-based silicon participants. Its computational abstraction separates study logic from participant implementation through standardized APIs for presenting information and collecting responses. We implement a researcher-facing authoring tool that reconstructs source-linked study descriptions from papers and supplementary materials, supports researcher review, and generates executable HumanStudyProgram artifacts. Researchers can then configure silicon participants, run the programs, and analyze results from aggregate findings to individual responses. We demonstrate the approach through study cases and evaluate the tool through a hands-on expert review with 12 social science researchers. All completed the workflow and identified potential uses in understanding published protocols, prototyping studies, and examining AI behavior. We aim to improve the reproducibility of human studies by reconstructing their documented procedures as programs that others can reuse and build upon.

papers.title: Competing Influence in LLM Populations: Budget Timing and Baseline Drift
papers.authors: Mehwish Nasim, Nicolas Fay
papers.what: [Explore] When competing campaigns target a population of large language model (LLM) agents, observed opinion changes may reflect both campaign influence and changes that would occur without intervention. We study how the timing of campaign expenditure and the population's own evolution sh
papers.summary: When competing campaigns target a population of large language model (LLM) agents, observed opinion changes may reflect both campaign influence and changes that would occur without intervention. We study how the timing of campaign expenditure and the population's own evolution shape outcomes in a network of persona-conditioned LLM agents that exchange and revise opinions in natural language. A proponent and a challenger are tasked with generating opposing messages under equal delivery budgets, while a separate stance probe measures opinions without influencing the simulation. Across eight claims, we compare single-campaign and competitive conditions against matched no-campaign runs, and evaluate all nine combinations of early, sustained, and late spending on a reference topic. Baseline stance drift varies substantially across claims and, on some, accounts for a sizeable fraction of apparent campaign effects. After accounting for this drift, the direction of observed campaign-associated changes aligns more closely with the claim's epistemic standing than with the campaigner's assigned role. Uninfluenced populations also consistently lose stance diversity, demonstrating that directional opinion change and convergence are distinct phenomena. In networks with two opinion-segregated communities, campaigns primarily reduce differences between communities rather than diversity within them. LLM campaign agents do not always argue for their assigned positions, particularly when these conflict with established evidence. Finally, campaign outcomes depend on the opponent's expenditure schedule: unlike a matched numerical bounded-confidence population receiving interventions at the same times and locations, the LLM population exhibits a payoff structure with no pure-strategy equilibrium.

papers.title: Spatial effects of Kuramoto modeling on the power-grid frequencies
papers.authors: Kristóf Benedek, Michelle T. Cirunay, Sangita Dutta, Attila Balogh et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Spatial coupling and heterogeneity can generate complex power-grid frequency dynamics. We investigate the contributions of spatial structure, intrinsic nonlinear dynamics, and external driving using the Kuramoto model (KM), with and without uncorrelated noise, and compare its pre
papers.summary: Spatial coupling and heterogeneity can generate complex power-grid frequency dynamics. We investigate the contributions of spatial structure, intrinsic nonlinear dynamics, and external driving using the Kuramoto model (KM), with and without uncorrelated noise, and compare its predictions with real-grid measurements. We analyse one month of 100 ms frequency measurements from 16 Hungarian transmission-grid sites and simulate the KM on a 387-node transmission network and two-dimensional lattices. The measured power spectra exhibit two scaling regimes, with exponents of approximately 1.63 and 2.23. One-second frequency increments decorrelate rapidly, while correlations of their local inverse variance decay slowly, initially as a power law, $τ^{-0.26(2)}$, up to 15 minutes. A superstatistical Gaussian mixture based on measured local variances captures much of the non-Gaussian increment distribution, but not the rare extreme events. We also estimate the non-stationary long-time frequency autocorrelation exponent. KM simulations on low-dimensional networks exhibit algebraically decaying autocorrelations and power spectra, consistent with the measurements and the Wiener-Khinchin relation in the steady state. On the heterogeneous transmission network, partial synchronization and frequency locking produce persistent spatial patterns and multi-peaked frequency distributions. However, neither deterministic KM dynamics nor independent Gaussian driving reproduces the measured spectra and increment statistics simultaneously. Moreover, empirical frequency fluctuations are largely shared across substations, whereas simulated fluctuations mainly reflect relative node motion. These findings suggest that spatially coupled nonlinear dynamics contribute to observed frequency fluctuations alongside external driving, including 15-minute power dispatches.

papers.title: Dynamic Graph Indexing for Label-Filtered Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.authors: Mengxu Jiang, Zhi Yang, Fangyuan Zhang, Yin Yang et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) over high-dimensional vectors is a core primitive in modern retrieval systems. In practice, objects are often also associated with labels (e.g., attributes or keywords), and retrieval must combine vector similarity with explicit label-ba
papers.summary: Approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS) over high-dimensional vectors is a core primitive in modern retrieval systems. In practice, objects are often also associated with labels (e.g., attributes or keywords), and retrieval must combine vector similarity with explicit label-based filtering, giving rise to label-filtered ANNS. This task is challenging because label filtering and ANNS favor very different index structures, selective filters fragment the admissible search space, and updates complicate index maintenance. To address these challenges, we propose DYLAN, a dynamic composite index for label-filtered ANNS supporting containment, overlap, and their conjunctions and disjunctions. DYLAN organizes label sets by shared prefixes in a frequency-ordered trie and selectively shares HNSW-style graph indices across trie-induced subsets, so that each trie region has a constant-factor covering index while each object participates in only logarithmically many indices. To mitigate fragmentation, DYLAN performs a cross-region multi-graph search that exploits ancestor-level indices as bridges between otherwise isolated trie regions. To support insertions, it adopts a threshold-based maintenance scheme that rebuilds shared indices only when necessary, yielding low amortized update cost. Extensive experiments with real data show that DYLAN consistently improves query throughput at comparable recall, by up to two orders of magnitude on challenging label-rich datasets, while retaining competitive memory, construction, and update costs.

papers.title: Reconfiguring System-Level Protection Through Bounded Delegation in RISC-V MCUs
papers.authors: Luís Cunha, José Martins, Manuel Rodríguez, Tiago Gomes et al.
papers.what: [Explore] MCU-based embedded and cyber-physical systems increasingly require protection policies to change at runtime as resources, software, and system composition evolve. Yet widely used COTS MCU protection mechanisms are still largely designed around statically established policies. Whi
papers.summary: MCU-based embedded and cyber-physical systems increasingly require protection policies to change at runtime as resources, software, and system composition evolve. Yet widely used COTS MCU protection mechanisms are still largely designed around statically established policies. While they can restrict which domains modify protection primitives, they generally do not constrain what policy an authorized domain may create. As a result, domains may expand protection rules beyond their intended scope or interfere with boundaries established by other domains. We identify bounded configuration authority as a missing primitive for secure dynamic policy evolution and introduce an ownership-aware model in which explicit ownership and rule containment bound both configuration authority and recursive delegation. Changes to active protection-rule ranges are validated before commit, preserving protection boundaries without extending the normal access-checking datapath. We implement the model in an open-source RISC-V World Checker integrated into a CVA6-based SoC. Our FPGA evaluation shows no degradation in access latency or operating frequency, with 7.1% LUT and 1.2% FF overhead for eight rules. In an OTA update case study, direct reconfiguration under delegated authority reduces policy-transition latency by 89.5% over hypervisor mediation and 94.6% over trusted firmware mediation, while preserving established authority boundaries. All artifacts will be open-sourced to support the evolution of RISC-V specifications and system-level protection designs.

papers.title: Perceived Agency During Agent-Avatar Control Transitions in Virtual Reality
papers.authors: Jingyi Zhang, Anthony Steed
papers.what: [Explore] Prior beliefs about whether a virtual human (VH) is controlled by a human or a computer can shape how users interpret and respond to its behaviour. As emerging hybrid VH systems allow control to transfer between human operators and computer programs during an ongoing interaction,
papers.summary: Prior beliefs about whether a virtual human (VH) is controlled by a human or a computer can shape how users interpret and respond to its behaviour. As emerging hybrid VH systems allow control to transfer between human operators and computer programs during an ongoing interaction, it remains unclear whether perceived agency updates with the actual controller or continues to reflect users' prior beliefs and first impressions. We investigated this question in a within-subject VR study with 24 participants across four conditions: always computer-controlled, computer-to-human, human-to-computer, and always human-controlled. We designed an interaction task in which participants acted as interviewers, asking the VHs a fixed set of questions. Before each interaction, participants were informed whether the VH was human- or computer-controlled, matching the actual controller at the beginning, but were unaware of possible control transitions. We found that perceived agency was strongly influenced by the controller presented at the beginning of the interaction, with no evidence of updating following the control transitions. Social evaluations including likeability and co-presence were generally higher in conditions where human control occurred later and covered a greater proportion of the interaction. The results suggest that prior beliefs and first impressions continued to shape perceived agency, whereas social evaluations were more sensitive to the VH's actual behaviour over the interaction.

papers.title: Suppression Is Not Erasure: Mechanistic Analysis and Reactivation Boundaries of Subspace Projection for LoRA Backdoor Defense
papers.authors: Junsheng Fu, Shuangshuang Gao
papers.what: [Explore] Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is the standard paradigm for customizing large language models, yet third-party LoRA adapters pose a supply-chain risk: modifying less than 1% of model parameters suffices to implant stealthy backdoors. Recent defenses project adapter weights onto estim
papers.summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is the standard paradigm for customizing large language models, yet third-party LoRA adapters pose a supply-chain risk: modifying less than 1% of model parameters suffices to implant stealthy backdoors. Recent defenses project adapter weights onto estimated backdoor subspaces, reporting near-zero static Attack Success Rates (ASR). We audit subspace-projection defenses across four model scales (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B) and three architectures (Qwen2.5, InternLM2.5, Spark). Constructively, module-wise rank-1 trigger-difference projection (k=1, alpha=1) reduces ASR from 60.4% to 0.0% on standard benchmarks and from 70.3% to 0.0% on a 1,000-sample uncontaminated suite (p = 3.055e-299, instruction-level p = 9.49e-16) in under 5 seconds end-to-end, and we prove via a spectral-gap bound why trigger-free calibration with benign polite suffixes aligns with u1(B) (median cosine 0.9048) and achieves 0.0% ASR without prior trigger knowledge. Our main contribution is a negative finding: static ASR reduction does not imply parameter erasure. Under 5-sample few-shot reactivation, every evaluated weight-editing defense rebounds (91.7%-100.0% ASR in 1 epoch for standard projections, Fine-Pruning, ANP, SVD truncation and Li & Kim's dual-end projection; 48.7% for our single-round dual variant), all reaching 100.0% by Epoch 2, with first-epoch loss up to 5.7x lower than training from scratch. Using an exact spectrum-preserving Haar orthogonal rotation control (Frobenius norm 10.0928 preserved to 1.70e-6) and N=1..6 cumulative Gram-Schmidt basis ablation, we decompose reactivation into residual trigger-difference coupling energy at Epoch 1 (Spearman rho = 0.986), base-model learnability at Epoch 2 (100%), and benign semantic direction conflict (41.7%).

papers.title: Simulating Vein Compressibility for Ultrasound-Guided Femoral Access: Speed, Accuracy, and Phantom Validation
papers.authors: Amit Manicka, Laurent Coulon, Darwin Ang, Michael Loushin et al.
papers.what: [Explore] In ultrasound-guided femoral access, probe pressure deforms the tissue and changes the vascular anatomy a robot observes. A simulator must reproduce these mechanics fast enough for robotic interaction, yet the computational effort needed for a clinically meaningful signal like ve
papers.summary: In ultrasound-guided femoral access, probe pressure deforms the tissue and changes the vascular anatomy a robot observes. A simulator must reproduce these mechanics fast enough for robotic interaction, yet the computational effort needed for a clinically meaningful signal like vein collapse before artery is unclear. We test the feasibility of a physics-based simulation in NVIDIA's Isaac Sim for Healthcare, with Stable Neo-Hookean tissue solved by Vertex Block Descent on one GPU. A simulation of a low-fidelity cylindrical benchtop phantom with known geometry and mechanical properties, pressed by a robot, predicted its artery within 5 percentage points at every depth. It matched the vein within 3 points through 11 mm of a 25.4 mm press and followed the collapse behavior of the low-fidelity physical phantom. Across element size, time step, and solver iterations, wall clock time per frame scaled linearly with solver work, but accuracy did not improve with more work. The chosen setting reduced solver time per frame by a factor of 976, from 29,700 ms to 30.4 ms, while remaining within 1.03 points of the finest reference setting. The physics solver alone took 30.4 ms per frame, while the full stack, including ultrasound and graphics rendering, took 56.4 ms per frame. Finally, when seeded with realistic literature-based mechanical properties, the digital leg model compressed the vein far more than the artery at every setting, reproducing the expected clinical signal of vein collapse before artery, which is used to distinguish them. In total, these results suggest that the NVIDIA Isaac Sim platform may be suitable for augmenting reinforcement learning training or online simulation for autonomous femoral access with ultrasound.

papers.title: Predictability of Collective Behavior in Networks of LLM Agents
papers.authors: Fabian Baumann, Michele Starnini
papers.what: [Explore] As AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact at scale, anticipating their collective behavior becomes necessary. Unlike humans, individual LLM agents can be probed in {controlled scenarios}; however, the predictability of their collective outcomes hing
papers.summary: As AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) increasingly interact at scale, anticipating their collective behavior becomes necessary. Unlike humans, individual LLM agents can be probed in {controlled scenarios}; however, the predictability of their collective outcomes hinges on what such measurements capture. We study information cascades on networks of LLM agents that decide whether to share a post given how many of their contacts have shared it. At the same fraction of sharing contacts, an agent's response depends on how many contacts it has and on the post. Responses that ignore the number of contacts mispredict the cascades, increasingly on heterogeneous networks, by an error we derive analytically and that network topology alone cannot reveal. Measured in context, the response predicts, through mean-field theory, the cascades of full LLM simulations, tipping points included. Anticipating the collective behavior of AI agents thus requires evaluating them in their local network context.

papers.title: Co-Creating Neurorehabilitation Technology Alongside Lived Experience Experts: A Participatory Design Workshop
papers.authors: Irene L. Y. Beck, Salvatore L. Cucinella, Johannes B. J. Bussmann, Natacha Léon et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Involving patients' lived experience (LE) early in neurorehabilitation technology design can improve the relevance and effectiveness of solutions, yet LE experts are often involved only when finished prototypes are tested. We present and evaluate a participatory design (PD) works
papers.summary: Involving patients' lived experience (LE) early in neurorehabilitation technology design can improve the relevance and effectiveness of solutions, yet LE experts are often involved only when finished prototypes are tested. We present and evaluate a participatory design (PD) workshop for early LE involvement, examine how LE contributions influence design processes and outcomes, and provide recommendations for similar approaches. We conducted a PD workshop at the 6th International Conference on NeuroRehabilitation. Five people who have had a stroke (LE experts) and 18 workshop attendees (including the LE experts' caregivers) were organized into five groups. Following the Discover, Define, and Develop phases of the Double Diamond model, each group used Journey Maps and Data Collection Notebooks to co-create a solution for an objective specified by an LE expert. Journey Maps were thematically analyzed, and group audio transcripts underwent structured extraction using a large language model. LE input shifted discussions from discipline-based assumptions toward priorities grounded in lived experience, including fear, confidence, sensory discomfort, fatigue, aesthetics, and independence. Narrow objectives, such as opening a blister pack, produced task-specific solutions, whereas broader objectives generated device concepts, including sensory feedback for cycling and a stimulation-equipped cooking splint. Satisfaction was high among attendees and LE experts. All workshop tools and protocols are shared to support adoption. The workshop offers a practical foundation for involving LE experts early in neurorehabilitation technology development. Future iterations should better capture psychological and social dimensions, allow more reflection, and include the full range of relevant stakeholders through sustained transdisciplinary engagement between researchers and the LE community.

papers.title: From LLM Hallucinations to Inspiration in Creative Work
papers.authors: Xinrui Lin, Heyan Huang, Shuning Zhang, Qi Wang et al.
papers.what: [Explore] Large language models (LLMs) can introduce unexpected ideas through hallucinations, yet little is known about when creative practitioners find these errors inspiring or how these judgments shape interactions. We conducted a retrospective qualitative study with 20 experienced prac
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) can introduce unexpected ideas through hallucinations, yet little is known about when creative practitioners find these errors inspiring or how these judgments shape interactions. We conducted a retrospective qualitative study with 20 experienced practitioners in research, design, and social media content creation, thematically analyzing 41 hallucination cases and 20 semi-structured interviews. Our framework links inspiration judgments of hallucinations based on goal relevance, task stage, content adaptability, and type-specific factors to behaviors across not-inspired, inspired-by, and inspired-to states. We characterize downstream interaction consequences, showing how hallucination-inspired experiences vary across creative stages and reshape role-differentiated trust, and propose these consequences as a dimension of hallucination evaluation. Finally, we derive design recommendations for stage-sensitive control of divergence and adherence, user-defined constraint priorities, differentiated hallucination labels, and salvage support for preserving useful ideas while correcting errors. These contributions deepen HCI understanding of hallucinations and responsible LLM design in creative work.
